claims.text: Increasing noble-metal content in near-equiatomic multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles accelerates high-temperature surface segregation.
Increasing noble-metal content accelerates nanoparticle sintering at high temperature.
Surface segregation and sintering compromise structural and chemical stability under catalytic and thermoelectric service conditions.
Lower noble-metal content maintains a more uniform phase and better catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Near-equiatomic multi-element alloys can initially exhibit a random, single-phase solid-solution structure.
Noble-metal-rich surface clusters promote localized sintering and phase instability.
Atoms in these nanoparticles become mobile at elevated temperatures.
Distinct noble-metal diffusion kinetics cause noble-metal atoms to migrate preferentially to nanoparticle surfaces.
Preferential noble-metal surface migration reduces solid-solution mixing stability.
Reduced mixing stability promotes sintering and possible phase separation.
Lower noble-metal concentration produces less segregation and therefore better retention of the single-phase structure and performance.
Higher noble-metal content will cause high-temperature XRD peak shifts and broadening indicative of structural change.
Higher noble-metal content will produce observable surface segregation in TEM/EDS.
Higher noble-metal content will degrade catalytic performance, including reducing conversion rates, relative to lower noble-metal content.
Lower noble-metal-content nanoparticles will largely preserve their phase and performance throughout the specified service-temperature ranges.
A moderate noble-metal-content baseline is known from prior work to form stable solid solutions at room temperature.
The proposed segregation mechanism should dominate at 773–1923 K in controlled atmospheres, although oxygen impurities and extreme alloying levels may alter the outcome.
